chunks: It was brought before Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him): six boys had been in the Euphrates, and one of them drowned. Three of them testified against two that those two had drowned him, and two testified against the three that they had drowned him. So he (peace be upon him) ruled that the blood money be divided into fifths: three-fifths upon the two, and two-fifths upon the three.

key_terms.الأخماس: Fifths (akhmas): the proportional division of the blood money — three-fifths on the two accused by three witnesses, two-fifths on the three accused by two witnesses — reflecting the principle that liability tracks the weight of testimony
key_terms.الدية: Blood money (diyah): the financial compensation paid to the victim's family in cases of wrongful death under Islamic law — the total amount due here was distributed proportionally rather than imposed on one group entirely
key_terms.غَرَّقَ: To drown (gharraqa): in this context used in the causative/intensive form, indicating the act of causing someone to drown, not merely drowning by accident

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali judge a case where conflicting testimonies about a drowning death in the Euphrates made it impossible to determine who was guilty?
ai.summary: This hadith records a legal case brought before Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) involving a drowning death in the Euphrates with mutually contradictory testimony. When three of the remaining five boys accused two of them of causing the drowning, while two boys in turn accused the three, Imam Ali resolved the impasse by distributing the blood money (diyah) proportionally to the number of witnesses against each group: three-fifths on those accused by three witnesses and two-fifths on those accused by two witnesses. This ruling illustrates Imam Ali's jurisprudential principle that, when contradictory evidence prevents certainty, liability is apportioned in proportion to the weight of testimony — a principle that became foundational in Shia fiqh.
